_comment: The AWS environment's single source of truth - the same role clusters/onprem/nodes.json plays
for the laptop and clusters/gcp/cluster.json plays for GKE (ADR-0008). Every value that could
disagree with reality comes from here, so it cannot disagree.
WHAT IS DELIBERATELY NOT IN THIS FILE: the AWS account ID. Same reasoning as the GCP billing
account ID - it is not a credential, knowing one grants nothing, but this repository is public
and it identifies a payment instrument. Nothing here needs it: an AWS Budget attaches to the
account the credentials belong to, so the API supplies it. `make aws-guardrails` prints the
account it is about to act on, from `aws sts get-caller-identity`, so the one thing a reader
needs to confirm is on screen without being in Git.
AND NO ACCESS KEYS, EVER. Credentials come from `aws configure` (or SSO) in the operator's own
~/.aws, never from a file in this repository - the same rule ADR-0018 enforced for GCP when it
refused to download a service-account key.
_region_comment: ap-south-1 (Mumbai) because it is nearest, so kubectl and the storefront are responsive - the
same reasoning that chose asia-south1 for GKE, and choosing the matching region is what makes
a latency or cost difference between the two substrates attributable to the substrate.
`make cost-check` already sweeps ap-south-1 and us-east-1. us-east-1 is in that list not
because anything is built there but because it is where a stray resource ends up when a tool
defaults its region, and a sweep that only looks where you meant to build is a sweep that
_az_comment: TWO AZs, AND THIS IS NOT A CHOICE - it is the first hard difference between EKS and GKE, and it
GKE's cluster is ZONAL on purpose (ADR-0003): one zone, free management fee, and the control
plane is Google's problem. EKS REQUIRES subnets in at least two Availability Zones to create a
cluster at all - the managed control plane places its ENIs across them - so 'zonal EKS' does
not exist and there is no cheaper single-AZ shape to choose.
WHAT THAT COSTS, and it is less than it looks: the control-plane fee is per cluster, not per AZ,
so the second AZ costs nothing by itself. The NODES are a different matter - cross-AZ traffic is
billed per GB in both directions - which is why node_group.single_az below pins every node into
the FIRST AZ. The subnets span two zones because EKS demands it; the workload does not.
The consequence worth stating rather than discovering: this cluster is NOT more available than
the GKE one despite having two zones' worth of subnets, because all the nodes are in one. That
is the honest trade for a lab, and it is the opposite of what the topology suggests.
_roadmap_divergence_comment: THIS FILE DESCRIBES AN EKS CLUSTER, AND THE ROADMAP ASKS FOR SOMETHING ELSE. Found 2026-11-04
while cross-referencing docs/reading.md against docs/roadmap.md, which is to say: by reading
the plan, which nobody had done since Module 08 started.
docs/roadmap.md, Module 09 - AWS: THE SELF-MANAGED ENVIRONMENT:
Terraform for spot EC2 instances (no NAT gateway); Ansible reused from Module 03 to
build the cluster; the AWS overlay; ONE EKS SESSION FOR COMPARISON, then destroyed.
So the primary AWS substrate is kubeadm on EC2 - the same ansible/roles/control_plane,
workers, cilium and kube_proxy_removal that build the laptop cluster - and EKS is a single
comparison session. ADR-0022 designed EKS as the primary and said nothing about kubeadm.
WHY IT MATTERS, beyond tidiness:
COST.    EKS charges $0.10/hour for the control plane with no free tier. kubeadm on EC2
charges nothing for a control plane because the control plane is an instance you
already pay for. The session estimate in ADR-0022 (~$0.20/hour) is therefore the
EKS number, and the primary path is closer to ~$0.10.
THE POINT OF THE MODULE. ADR-0001 asks for six concrete differences between substrates,
and GKE already supplied the managed-control-plane contrast. A second managed
cluster measures the same axis twice. The self-managed one is what tests whether
Layers 0 and 1 port - the Ansible that has only ever run against libvirt VMs.
WHAT IS KEPT: the budget guardrail, the region, the AZ facts, and the instance type - all of
which apply to both shapes. m6a.large is still right and t3.* is still the trap. What needs
rewriting is the node_group block below, which is EKS-managed-node-group shaped, and ADR-0022
Decision 5's claim that two AZs are forced - that is an EKS constraint and does not bind a
kubeadm cluster on plain EC2.
SECOND INSTANCE OF THIS EXACT MISTAKE. STATUS.md already records one: a parking-lot entry
called something 'Module 08's opening move' and was believed on a later read, when the
roadmap said otherwise. The roadmap is the plan; a document written later is not an
amendment to it just because it is more recent.
_cluster_name_comment: `platform`, the same name as the GKE cluster and the on-prem one, deliberately. The kubectl
CONTEXT is what must differ, and `make aws-kubeconfig` names it `aws-platform` to sit beside
`gcp-platform` and `onprem-admin` - because the generated EKS context name is the cluster ARN,
which is long enough that a prompt truncates it, and a truncated context next to two others is
how a command lands on the wrong cluster (the GKE module learned this the same way).
_budget_comment: ADR-0003 Decision 3: this must exist BEFORE the first AWS resource, which is why it is a
separate Terraform state in terraform/aws/guardrails and a separate `make aws-guardrails`.
A guardrail applied in the same run as the thing it guards is not a guardrail.
$5 AND NOT ₹400, and the difference is not just currency. AWS Budgets are denominated in the
account's billing currency, which for an account created with a US-dollar payment profile is
USD - and a budget whose currency does not match the account's is rejected rather than
converted. ₹400 is about $4.50, so $5 is the same order of magnitude by accident rather than
by conversion; if the account turns out to bill in INR, change the currency and the amount
WHY THE NUMBER IS SMALL ENOUGH TO MEAN SOMETHING: an EKS session is roughly $0.20/hour (see
the node comment), so $5 is about 25 hours of cluster time. A budget set at $50 would never
fire on a lab that is supposed to run three hours a week, and an alarm that never fires is
AND WHY IT MATTERS MORE HERE THAN ON GCP: on the AWS free account plan there is NO spend cap
available - the monthly project spend limit that actually PAUSES resources exists only after
upgrading to the paid plan. So on the free plan this budget is not one guardrail among several,
it is the only one, and it alerts rather than stops. `make aws-down` is the control.
_instance_type_comment: m6a.large: 2 DEDICATED vCPU, 8 GB. NOT t3.large, NOT t3.medium, and that is the whole point of
this comment.
THE t3 FAMILY IS BURSTABLE, which is the same trap as GCP's e2-medium that cost Module 08 a
cluster rebuild. e2-medium is listed as 2 vCPU, guarantees one, and GKE reported 940m
allocatable - so six of ShopVerse's eight pods stayed Pending with 'Insufficient cpu' and the
capacity estimate was wrong by 2.05x. t3 instances work the same way: a baseline percentage of
a vCPU plus CPU credits, and the Kubernetes scheduler schedules against neither the baseline
nor the credits - it schedules against what the kubelet reports as allocatable.
The failure shape is what makes this worth pinning rather than measuring: a burstable node
does not fail at creation. It creates, reports Ready, and then refuses to schedule - so the
symptom arrives one layer away from the cause, in the tenant's Application.
m6a is AMD and is the cheaper of the dedicated 2 vCPU / 8 GB families; m5.large, m6i.large and
m7a.large are the same shape at different prices. WHAT HAS NOT BEEN VERIFIED: that m6a.large is
offered in ap-south-1. Written down rather than assumed, because three pins in this repository
have been wrong from memory. Ask the API, do not read a blog:
aws ec2 describe-instance-type-offerings --region ap-south-1 \
--filters Name=instance-type,Values=m6a.large --query 'InstanceTypeOfferings[].Location'
If it comes back empty, change this one value to m5.large and re-apply. The failure is loud and
costs one edit, which is the cheap direction to be wrong in - unlike the burstable mistake,
which is silent.
SPOT, for the same ~60-90% discount the GKE pool uses, and with the same trade: an instance can
be reclaimed at two minutes' notice. Module 11 uses that deliberately. What differs from GKE is
the interruption notice mechanism, which is a real per-substrate difference rather than a
cosmetic one.
MAX PODS PER NODE IS AN AWS-ONLY CEILING, and it is worth knowing before it bites. The VPC CNI
gives each pod a real VPC IP from an ENI, and an instance type caps how many ENIs and IPs it
gets - m6a.large is 3 ENIs x 10 IPv4, so about 29 pods per node against GKE's 110. Two nodes is
~58 pods for ShopVerse's 8 plus the platform, which fits; a third tenant is where this starts to
matter. GKE has no equivalent limit because its pods come from a secondary CIDR, not from ENIs.
_networking_comment: PUBLIC SUBNETS WITH PUBLIC IPs ON THE NODES, which looks wrong and is the same decision the GKE
cluster made for the same reason (ADR-0019 Decision 3).
ShopVerse's seven images are on ghcr.io. ADR-0003 forbids NAT gateways - at roughly $0.045/hour
plus per-GB processing, a NAT gateway is the single most expensive idle thing in either cloud -
and a node in a private subnet with no NAT cannot reach ghcr.io at all. VPC endpoints cover
AWS's own APIs and nothing else, exactly as Private Google Access does.
So: public subnets, public IPs, and security groups as the boundary. A public IP is about
$0.005/hour each, the same order as GCP's, which is the other reason ADR-0003's target reads
Mirroring the images into ECR is the better end state and is genuinely free within ECR's
storage allowance; it costs a mirroring step and a global.imageRegistry override in the aws
overlay, which is what the overlay mechanism is for. Parked here as it is parked for GCP, so
the two substrates carry the same debt rather than diverging quietly.
AND THE ONE THAT HAS NO GCP EQUIVALENT: ADR-0003 forbids leaving a load balancer running, and
on AWS the ingress layer is an ALB or NLB created by a controller INSIDE the cluster - so it is
an object Terraform never made, exactly like the GKE Gateway's forwarding rule. ADR-0021 learned
that ordering twice (the forwarding rule, then an orphaned Persistent Disk) and the rule is
written down: anything a controller in the cluster created must be removed while that controller
is still alive. `make aws-down` owes this from its first line, not as an amendment.
